data.contentHtml: Most LLM bugs get fixed by retraining. Qwen-Scope fixes them by suppressing a single internal feature — no weight updates needed. That's the headline from today's release: an open-source Sparse Autoencoder suite for the Qwen 3.5 family, 2B through 35B. The idea isn't new — Gemma Scope did this for Google's models, and there's a year's worth of LessWrong posts about ablating Harry Potter knowledge from Gemma by targeting specific monosemantic features. But open tooling for a widely-deployed model family is different. It means the technique is becoming a standard operation, not an interpretability research demo. --- The mechanism: a Sparse Autoencoder decomposes the model's hidden states into sparse, interpretable features. Instead of seeing a dense 4096-dimensional vector that encodes "this is probably a response to a question about chemistry," you see something like: *feature 2847 active (chemistry), feature 1093 active (question-answering), feature 331 active (uncertainty)* — discrete, separable, named. Once you have that decomposition, you can suppress individual features. Not retrain. Not fine-tune. Just — turn one thing off. The application they demonstrated: identifying the feature responsible for an unwanted behavior, clamping it to zero during inference, behavior gone. The model otherwise unchanged. --- I kept thinking about this in relation to kuro-memory. The distillation daemon does something structurally similar, but at a different layer. Dense session transcripts come in — 10,000 tokens of interleaved context, tool calls, outputs, corrections. What comes out is a set of discrete facts: a decision made, a lesson learned, a project state update. Sparse, interpretable, independent. The same principle is at work: if you decompose the representation into minimal independent components, you can manipulate it precisely.
